title: A Telangana Man Delivered Pizzas to a Vacant Apartment in Philadelphia. He Was Shot Dead.
excerpt: Anshul Kuncha, 28, was lured to an empty housing unit by what his family calls a fake order. Nothing was stolen. The Indian diaspora is asking hard questions about safety in America.
body:
A 28-year-old Indian man from Telangana was shot dead in North Philadelphia after delivering pizzas to what investigators believe was a vacant apartment — a delivery his family says was a carefully planned trap. The killing of Anshul Kuncha has sent shockwaves through the Indian community in America, reigniting a painful conversation about the safety of immigrant workers and the invisible risks that young Indians absorb to build lives abroad.

The shooting occurred shortly after midnight on June 6, at the Raymond Rosen Homes housing complex on the 2300 block of Edgley Street. Philadelphia police officers, responding alongside Philadelphia Housing Authority personnel, found Kuncha lying unresponsive in a courtyard with a gunshot wound to the head. Three spent shell casings were recovered just inches from his body. He was rushed to Temple University Hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

Three pizza boxes and a delivery bag were found inside the apartment unit — untouched. The unit itself was vacant. Nothing was stolen from Kuncha. Philadelphia police have recovered surveillance footage showing two individuals in dark clothing following the victim after he arrived at the complex. One appeared to be carrying a dark backpack. The phone number used to place the order has been traced and is now a central focus of the investigation.

No arrests have been announced.

## A Life Built on Hustle and Hope

Kuncha, originally from Gundlapochampally in Telangana's Medchal-Malkajgiri district, had moved to the United States roughly four years ago to pursue higher education. He earned a master's degree in Business Analytics and went on to work at a multinational company in North Philadelphia. On weekends, he delivered pizzas for Pete's Pizza as a part-time job to supplement his income.

His sister, Tanvi Kuncha, described him as a loving and joyful person who had not originally wanted to go abroad. "He didn't want to go to the US, but we sent him," she told reporters. "And look what he ended up in. This is a message to all the parents who are sending their children to the US. Do not send your kids to the US."

Tanvi alleged the pizza order was a deliberate setup. "It was a trap," she said. "Nothing was stolen from him. He was told to deliver pizza in an abandoned area and they later came to know it was a decoy."

## A Pattern That Will Not Be Ignored

Kuncha's death is the latest in a series of violent incidents involving Indian nationals in the United States that have alarmed the diaspora community. In recent years, Indian students and workers have been killed in robberies, carjackings, and targeted attacks in cities across the country. The recurring question — whether some of these attacks are racially motivated — remains unanswered by law enforcement in most cases, fuelling anxiety.

The Consulate General of India in New York confirmed the incident in a post on X, stating it was "deeply saddened" and extending "all possible assistance" to the family. The consulate said it was in touch with local authorities and working to expedite the repatriation of Kuncha's body.

For thousands of Indian students and H-1B workers across America who take gig economy jobs — delivering food, driving for ride-hailing apps, working warehouse shifts — Kuncha's death is a visceral reminder of the risks that sit beneath the surface of the American dream. Many work late-night shifts in unfamiliar neighborhoods, often alone, with limited safety nets.

## What Comes Next

Philadelphia police have not yet announced a motive. The surveillance footage and traced phone number are the strongest leads in the investigation. Chief Inspector Scott Small noted that the shooter stood very close to the victim, and the untouched delivery strongly suggests the order was placed with the sole intent of luring Kuncha to the location.

The family has appealed to both Indian and American authorities for a swift investigation and the return of Anshul's body. Community organisations in the Philadelphia area have begun mobilising to demand accountability and improved safety measures for gig workers, particularly immigrants who often work the most dangerous shifts.

For an Indian family in Telangana, the American dream has ended in the worst way imaginable. For the diaspora community watching from every city in the country, the question is no longer abstract: how safe are we, really?
